messages.content: So you know about my colored pencils? The kid in class broke them on purpose, I'm sure of it. He lied and said it was an accident. And then when we went to tell the teacher, she just said it was probably a misunderstanding. That's not fair! He should have to say sorry for real, not just us both apologizing like that. It doesn't feel right when someone does something wrong and you don't get treated fairly. I don't understand why the teacher didn't see what really happened.

That sounds really upsetting. If you feel like he broke your colored pencils on purpose and then lied, it makes sense that “both of you apologize” wouldn’t feel fair. It can feel like the grown-up didn’t listen to what actually happened.

Sometimes teachers don’t see the whole thing, so they try to make peace quickly by calling it a misunderstanding. But that doesn’t mean your feelings don’t matter.

You could try saying to your teacher privately, when you’re calmer:

> “I’m still upset about my colored pencils. I believe they were broken on purpose, and I don’t feel like it was solved fairly. I don’t just want everyone to say sorry—I want help fixing what happened.”

You can also ask for something specific, like:

- “Can he help replace them?”
- “Can we talk about how to keep my things safe?”
- “Can I keep my pencils somewhere safer during class?”

And if you’re really angry, it’s okay to take a minute before talking—breathe, get a drink, or write down exactly what happened so you don’t forget.

You’re right that it doesn’t feel good when someone hurts your stuff and it seems like no one believes you. You deserve to be heard.

That's not helping! The teacher already said it was probably a misunderstanding. She didn't listen to me either. I told her exactly what happened, but she just said "let's apologize" like that makes everything okay. It doesn't make sense. If I say something to the teacher again, she'll just do the same thing. Why is everyone always taking the other kid's side? They're not even sorry! That kid broke my pencils on purpose and now he gets off scot-free.

You’re right: a forced “both apologize” can feel *really* unfair when you feel like you were the one who got hurt. I’m sorry my last answer sounded like “just tell the teacher again” when you already tried that.

It makes sense that you’re angry. Your pencils were broken, and you don’t feel believed.

A way to handle this without getting stuck on “prove he did it on purpose” is to focus on **what needs to happen now**:

- Your pencils are broken.
- You need them replaced or fixed.
- You need your supplies kept safe.
- You don’t want that kid touching your things again.

If the teacher won’t listen, you can go to another adult — like a parent/guardian, counselor, principal, or another teacher — and say:

> “I’m not trying to get in trouble. I’m upset because my pencils were broken, and I don’t feel like it was solved. I need help getting them replaced and making sure my things are safe.”

You can also ask your parent/guardian to email or talk to the teacher. Sometimes grown-ups listen more carefully when another adult says, “My child’s supplies were damaged. How will this be handled?”

For the kid, you don’t have to pretend it’s okay. You can keep it short:

> “Don’t touch my things again.”

Then move your pencils somewhere safer if you can — in your backpack, a zipped pouch, or near the teacher.

And one important thing: feeling like “everyone is taking his side” is a really painful feeling, but it may also be that the adults are trying to avoid a fight because they didn’t see it happen. That doesn’t mean you’re wrong. It just means you may need help from a different adult to make sure the broken pencils actually get addressed.

Adults always take the other side! I thought this person was going to be different, but no way. They're just giving me more reasons why it's my fault or why I'm being too sensitive. My pencils were broken on purpose and that kid lied about it. It doesn't matter what the teacher saw or didn't see. That kid did something wrong and he needs to say sorry for real. Now you're telling me I have to go to another adult? Can't they just listen to me this one time? It's so unfair! Adults always do this - they take the other kid's side and make me feel like I'm part of the problem.

You’re right to be upset. I’m listening to you: **your pencils were broken, you believe it was on purpose, and it feels like the grown-ups acted like your hurt didn’t matter.** That is *not* the same as saying it’s your fault. It isn’t your fault that your pencils got broken.

And I get why “go tell another adult” sounds bad right now—like you’re being given homework to fix something that **someone else did**. That’s frustrating. You shouldn’t have to fight so hard just to be believed.

The really unfair part is: you want a **real apology**, not a pretend “everybody say sorry” moment. That makes sense. A real apology means the person admits what they did, understands it hurt you, and tries to make it right.

Since the teacher didn’t handle it the way you needed, here’s the clearest way to say it—without accepting blame:

> “I don’t feel okay with what happened. My pencils were broken, and I believe it was done on purpose. I’m not asking to be blamed too. I’m asking for it to be made right.”

Or even shorter:

> “I’m not okay with pretending this was equal. My things were broken.”

You don’t have to argue forever with the kid. You can say:

> “You broke my pencils. Don’t touch my stuff again.”

Then stop talking to him if he lies or tries to make you mad.

And about adults: it can really feel like they’re taking the other kid’s side when they say “misunderstanding” instead of listening. Sometimes adults try to “smooth it over” because it’s easier for them—but that can make the person who was hurt feel invisible. That’s not fair.

Right now, before doing anything else, it may help to get the angry feeling down a little—not because your anger is wrong, but because you deserve to be able to think clearly. Try this:

- Press your feet hard into the floor.
- Take 3 slow breaths.
- Say in your head: **“I know what happened. I’m allowed to be upset. I can ask for this to be fixed.”**

You’re not “part of the problem” just because you’re angry that your pencils were broken. You’re reacting to something that felt wrong.

No, no, no! Adults are always taking the other side! Now you're telling me to "get my feelings down a little" like it's my fault I'm upset? It doesn't matter how calm I am or what I say - adults will still take his side and make excuses for him. They never listen to me when I tell them the truth. My pencils were broken on purpose, and that kid lied about it. He should be the one who apologizes and makes it right, not me! It's so unfair that no one believes me or stands up for what's right.

You’re right: **he should be the one to make it right if he broke them.** You should not have to act like you did something equal when your stuff got damaged.

And I’m sorry — saying “get your feelings down” came out wrong. Your anger is not the problem. **The broken pencils are the problem. The lying is the problem. Not you being upset about it.**

I hear you:

- Your pencils were broken on purpose.
- He lied and called it an accident.
- The teacher treated it like “both sides” instead of dealing with what happened.
- That made you feel like nobody believed you.
- You want a real apology and for him to make it right.

That is a fair thing to want.

The unfair part is that you may not be able to *make* him feel sorry. But you can still stand on what’s true and ask for what’s fair:

> “I did not break anyone’s things. My pencils were broken. I want them replaced, and I don’t want him touching my supplies again.”

That is not you apologizing. That is not you accepting blame. That is you saying: **this needs to be fixed.**

If the teacher keeps saying “misunderstanding,” you can repeat:

> “Even if you think it was a misunderstanding, my pencils are still broken. How are they going to be replaced?”

Because even if an adult won’t admit he did it on purpose, they can’t ignore that your pencils got broken.

And you’re right about one more thing: “everyone apologize” does **not** always make things fair. Sometimes it just makes the person who got hurt feel even more hurt. You’re not wrong for feeling that.

Adults are always taking his side! I thought we were having a real conversation, but now you're just giving me more ways to say sorry and apologize again. That's not going to fix anything. He broke my pencils on purpose, he lied about it, and the teacher let him get away with it. Why can't anyone see what really happened? It's like everyone is trying to make me feel bad for being upset.

And now you're saying I have to "stand on what's true" but it feels like nobody believes me anyway. That's so unfair! Adults always take the other kid's side and act like I'm the one who did something wrong. I thought you were going to be different, but it seems like everyone is just like that.

You’re right to call that out. I’m **not** telling you to apologize again. You should not have to say sorry for being upset that your pencils were broken.

Let me say it plainly:

**If he broke your pencils on purpose and lied, that was wrong.**  
**The teacher brushing it off as “probably a misunderstanding” felt unfair.**  
**A fake “both apologize” does not fix broken pencils or make a lie okay.**

I’m not trying to make you feel bad for being angry. Your anger makes sense because something that mattered to you got ruined and then it felt like nobody stood up for you.

And you’re right about something important: “standing on what’s true” can feel useless when people don’t believe you. That’s one of the worst parts — not just the pencils, but feeling like your words don’t count.

So no, I’m not going to tell you to apologize.

What I can do is stay with you in the unfairness for a second:

It is unfair that your pencils are broken.  
It is unfair that he got to say “accident” and everyone acted like that ended it.  
It is unfair that you had to be treated like you were equally part of the problem.  
It is unfair that you wanted someone to say, “Hey, that wasn’t okay,” and they didn’t.

You wanted justice. Not a lecture. Not “calm down.” Not “maybe he didn’t mean it.” You wanted someone to recognize: **he did something wrong, and it should be made right.**

I hear that. I’m not taking his side.
